title: pauseWithdraw shrinks user.amount without updating reward debt or pool, bricking the position on the next stake/withdraw/claim
description: pauseWithdraw decrements user.amount (L285) and totalStaked (L286) but does NOT update userInfo.phUSDDebt / userInfo.stableDebt, and skips _updatePool entirely (the function is a bare emergency exit). The reward-debt fields therefore retain values computed against the user's PRE-withdrawal (larger) amount. After the contract is unpaused, the very next call into _claimRewards (reached by stake L337, withdraw L373, or claim L424) computes pendingPhUSDAmount = (userDetails.amount * accPhUSDPerShare) / PRECISION - userDetails.phUSDDebt (L493) and the analogous stable line (L498). Because userDetails.amount is now strictly smaller than the amount the debt was anchored to, the subtrahend (phUSDDebt) exceeds the minuend, producing an unsigned underflow that reverts (Solidity 0.8 checked arithmetic). The branch fires whenever accPhUSDPerShare/accStablePerShare are unchanged or grow by less than the debt gap, which is the normal case immediately post-pause.
impact: Any user who performs a partial pauseWithdraw permanently bricks their own remaining position: every subsequent stake, withdraw, and claim for that user reverts. Their leftover stake and all accrued rewards become unrecoverable through the normal flow (only another full pauseWithdraw, which itself forfeits rewards, lets them exit principal). This is a loss-of-funds / function-availability defect that survives unchanged from V1.
exploitPath: 1) Contract paused (pauser calls pause). 2) User calls pauseWithdraw(partial) -> user.amount shrinks, debt unchanged. 3) Contract unpaused. 4) User calls claim()/withdraw()/stake() -> _claimRewards underflows at L493/L498 -> revert. Position is stuck.
lawBasis: Law 1 (no exploits / loss of user funds and bricked positions).

title: pendingPhUSD / pendingStable views revert (underflow) for a position after a partial pauseWithdraw
description: Same stale-debt root cause as CODE-001 manifesting in the view functions. pendingPhUSD returns (userDetails.amount * _accPhUSDPerShare) / PRECISION - userDetails.phUSDDebt (L536) and pendingStable returns the analogous expression (L557). After a partial pauseWithdraw shrinks userDetails.amount while leaving phUSDDebt/stableDebt anchored to the larger pre-withdrawal amount, the subtraction underflows and the view reverts instead of returning a value.
impact: Off-chain integrations, front-ends, and on-chain callers that read pendingPhUSD/pendingStable for an affected user get a revert rather than a number, degrading UX and breaking any contract that depends on these views for accounting. No direct fund loss beyond CODE-001.
exploitPath: Partial pauseWithdraw -> call pendingPhUSD(user) or pendingStable(user) -> arithmetic underflow revert at L536 / L557.
lawBasis: Law 1 (availability of read path that integrators rely on; same defect class as CODE-001).

title: pauseWithdraw has no MINIMUM_STAKE dust handling, leaving sub-minimum positions
description: Unlike withdraw (which forces a full exit when the remaining balance would fall below MINIMUM_STAKE, L379-382), pauseWithdraw performs a raw user.amount -= amount with no dust guard. A user can leave an arbitrarily small residual position (e.g. 1 wei) that is below MINIMUM_STAKE, weakening the MINIMUM_STAKE invariant the protocol otherwise enforces on the normal withdraw path.
impact: Sub-minimum dust positions persist, weakening the first-depositor / minimum-stake invariant. Combined with CODE-001 the dust residue is also unrecoverable. Low severity: no direct theft, primarily an invariant-weakening / accounting-hygiene issue.
exploitPath: Pause -> pauseWithdraw(user.amount - 1) -> residual 1 wei position below MINIMUM_STAKE remains.
lawBasis: Law 2 (invariant INV-6 minimum-stake not upheld on the emergency path).

title: pauseWithdraw silently forfeits accrued rewards and orphans per-share residue (forfeiture-by-design)
description: pauseWithdraw exits principal without ever calling _updatePool or _claimRewards, so a user's accrued phUSD/stable rewards at the time of emergency exit are forfeited, and the corresponding per-share accumulator residue is orphaned (left to be diluted across remaining stakers). No reward-related event is emitted; only EmergencyWithdrawal (L290) fires. This was previously blessed under the KI-4 forfeiture-by-design known issue and is unchanged in V2.
impact: Users who emergency-exit lose pending rewards with no on-chain signal. Accepted design trade-off; retained as QA for completeness.
exploitPath: Pause -> user pauseWithdraw -> pending rewards forfeited, no reward event emitted.
lawBasis: Law 2 (documented design choice; QA-level spec note).

title: emergencyTransfer + setPauser(0) is a permanent-lock footgun: drained balance bricks pauseWithdraw and a zero pauser blocks unpause
description: emergencyTransfer sweeps the entire phUSD and rewardToken balance to a recipient (L255-260) and then _pause()s (L262), but it does NOT zero totalStaked or any userInfo entry. After the sweep the contract holds no phUSD, so pauseWithdraw's safeTransfer (L288) reverts for every user (insufficient contract balance) even though their userInfo.amount is still non-zero. Recovery requires unpause, but unpause (L217) requires msg.sender == pauser, and setPauser (L224-226) has no zero-address guard. If the owner has set pauser to address(0) (a configuration setPauser explicitly accepts), no address can ever satisfy the unpause check, so the contract is permanently paused AND drained -> every user position is permanently locked with no exit.
impact: Owner footgun (non-obvious): a competent, non-malicious owner who has zeroed the pauser (a supported, sometimes-recommended 'disable pausing' configuration) and later invokes emergencyTransfer would be surprised that the combination is an irreversible total lock of all user funds. This is an operational hazard, not a malicious-owner vector.
exploitPath: Footgun trigger: setPauser(0) at some point + later emergencyTransfer(recipient) -> contract paused with no pauser to unpause and no phUSD to satisfy pauseWithdraw -> all positions permanently frozen. Mitigation: add a zero-address guard on setPauser and/or zero accounting in emergencyTransfer; never zero the pauser while positions exist.
lawBasis: Law 3 (non-obvious owner footgun enabling permanent fund lock; in scope).

title: setPauser lacks a zero-address guard and emits no event
description: setPauser assigns pauser = _pauser with no zero-address validation and emits no event. Setting pauser to address(0) silently disables both pause() and unpause() (both require msg.sender == pauser), and is the enabling precondition for the permanent-lock footgun in CODE-005. The absence of an event also reduces off-chain observability of a security-critical role change.
impact: Loss of pause/unpause controllability when pauser is zeroed, and degraded monitoring of a privileged-role change. Low on its own; compounds CODE-005.
exploitPath: setPauser(0) -> pause()/unpause() become uncallable; no event for monitors.

title: RateUpdated event is declared but never emitted
description: The RateUpdated(uint256 newRate, uint256 newBalance) event is declared at L126 but is never emitted anywhere in PhlimboV2 (grep confirms the only reward-related emits are RewardCollected at L311 and DepletionDurationUpdated at L210). Dead event declaration; the rate changes in collectReward and setDepletionDuration are signalled by other events, so consumers expecting RateUpdated never receive it.
impact: Off-chain consumers that subscribe to RateUpdated will never see it; dead code. No security impact. QA.

title: setDesiredAPY commit branch does not clear pendingAPYBps / pendingAPYBlockNumber
description: On commit, setDesiredAPY sets apySetInProgress = false (L188) but leaves the stale pendingAPYBps and pendingAPYBlockNumber values in storage (they are only overwritten on the next preview, L179-180). getPendingAPYInfo (L582) therefore reports stale pending values after a commit even though no set is in progress. Because the preview/commit gate keys off apySetInProgress and an exact bps + block-window match (L173-175), the stale values do not cause an incorrect commit, but the reported pending state is misleading.
impact: Misleading getPendingAPYInfo output (stale pending APY/block reported as if relevant) after a committed APY change. No logic exploit; the gating uses apySetInProgress. Low / housekeeping.
exploitPath: Preview setDesiredAPY(x) -> commit setDesiredAPY(x) -> getPendingAPYInfo still returns x and the old block number with apySetInProgress=false.

title: Cross-function reentrancy lever is closed by the shared ReentrancyGuard (refuted candidate)
description: REFUTATION of the L-09 carryover. All value-handling entrypoints (stake L323, withdraw L363, claim L407, collectReward L298) are nonReentrant on the same OZ ReentrancyGuard. The new hook calls (L353/L398/L429) and the _claimRewards mint/transfer (L495/L500) all execute inside that single guard, so a malicious or buggy hook (or token callback) attempting to re-enter any staking function reverts on the guard. The hook also fires AFTER all state mutations and token movements, so even absent the guard there is no stale-state window for the hook to exploit on the entered function. pauseWithdraw is not nonReentrant but performs a single checked decrement + plain ERC20 transfer with no callback surface and is msg.sender-only. The cross-contract reentrancy lever is therefore closed; this is recorded as informational/resolved, not a live finding.
exploitPath: Attempted hook re-entry into stake/withdraw/claim -> ReentrancyGuard reverts.

title: Arbitrary stake-for-victim griefing is closed by the new caller==user||migrator auth (refuted/resolved candidate)
description: REFUTATION/RESOLUTION of L-10. In V1, stake(amount, recipient) had no caller restriction, so any third party could stake on a victim's behalf and re-anchor the victim's reward-debt clock (griefing). V2 adds require(msg.sender == user || msg.sender == migrator) at L326 (and the same gate on withdraw L365 and claim L409). A non-authorized third party can no longer touch another user's position, closing the arbitrary-griefer vector. The migrator is a trusted role (Law 3); its standing power is addressed separately in CODE-013.
exploitPath: Third party calls stake(amount, victim) -> reverts 'Not authorized' (L326).

title: A reverting hook bricks stake/withdraw/claim contract-wide (hook-liveness footgun)
description: The optional hook is invoked unconditionally (when set) at the end of stake (L353-355), withdraw (L398-400), and claim (L429-431), with no try/catch. If the configured hook reverts -- whether by a bug, by depending on external state that later becomes unavailable, by being self-pausable, or by running out of gas -- it reverts the entire outer call. This couples core staking liveness to the correctness/availability of an auxiliary side-effect contract. The owner is trusted to set a non-malicious hook (Law 3, IPhlimboHook docstring), but a hook that reverts UNEXPECTEDLY after deployment is a non-obvious consequence a competent owner would be surprised by. Mitigating factor: pauseWithdraw (L280) explicitly invokes no hook, so IF the contract is paused users retain a principal-only emergency exit; however that exit forfeits rewards (CODE-004) and is unavailable while the contract is unpaused.
impact: Owner footgun: a hook that begins reverting freezes all stake/withdraw/claim activity until the owner calls setHook(0) or the pauser pauses to enable the (lossy) pauseWithdraw escape. Denial of service on core functionality; no direct theft. The blast radius is the whole user base, not a single position.
exploitPath: Footgun trigger: setHook(H); H later reverts (bug / external dependency / self-pause) -> all stake/withdraw/claim revert at L353/L398/L431. Recovery: owner setHook(0), or pauser pause() then users pauseWithdraw (principal only). Recommendation: wrap hook calls in try/catch (or a bounded-gas call that ignores hook reverts) so a faulty hook cannot brick core staking.
lawBasis: Law 3 (non-obvious owner footgun) / Law 1 (availability of core functions).

title: Strict-equality balance preconditions let any third party brick settleDebt/migrateDeposits with a 1-wei dust transfer (repeatable, permissionless DoS)
description: settleDebt requires usdc.balanceOf(this) == totalUSDC (L159) AND phUSD.balanceOf(this) == totalPHUSD_deposited (L160-163); migrateDeposits requires phUSD.balanceOf(this) == totalPHUSD_deposited (L207-210). All three are strict equalities. ERC20 transfers are permissionless and have no recipient-side hook, so ANY third party can transfer 1 wei of USDC or phUSD directly to the migrator, making balanceOf strictly greater than the stored total. Both functions then revert on the precondition for every subsequent call. The contract has no mechanism to reconcile or skim an over-balance: withdrawAll (L249-262) drains everything to the owner but explicitly does NOT adjust totals or iterators (L245 comment), so after a withdraw the balance is 0 != total and the functions still revert; resuming requires re-funding the migrator to EXACTLY the stored total, at which point a griefer can re-send 1 wei and re-brick. The attack costs ~1 wei + gas, requires no authorization, and is indefinitely repeatable.
impact: Permissionless, near-zero-cost, repeatable denial of service on the entire V1->V2 migration. An attacker can stall settlement of V1 reward obligations (USDC/phUSD owed to users) and the re-staking of V1 deposits for as long as they choose, with each owner recovery attempt re-grievable. This blocks users from receiving owed rewards and from having their stake migrated -- a protocol-availability failure on a critical one-shot operation, with no safe automated recovery in the current code.
exploitPath: 1) Owner seeds + funds migrator to exactly totalUSDC / totalPHUSD_deposited. 2) Attacker transfers 1 wei USDC (or phUSD) to the migrator. 3) settleDebt / migrateDeposits revert with 'USDC balance mismatch' / 'phUSD balance mismatch'. 4) Owner withdrawAll + re-fund-exact -> attacker repeats step 2. Fix: replace == with >= preconditions (the loop logic already decrements totals consistently and caps work by iterator, so an over-balance is harmless), or snapshot/skim the surplus.
lawBasis: Law 1 (third-party permissionless DoS on a critical protocol operation).

title: setMigrator is not auto-revoked after migration: the migrator retains standing authority to route any user's stake and rewards to itself
description: Once PhlimboV2.setMigrator(M) is set (required for migration, L232-236), M can call withdraw(amount, user) and claim(user) for ANY user at any time. withdraw sends the withdrawn principal to msg.sender (the migrator, L392) and routes the auto-claimed rewards to msg.sender (L373 -> _claimRewards beneficiary = msg.sender, L495/L500); claim likewise routes rewards to msg.sender (L424). The migrator role is never automatically revoked when migration completes -- there is no lifecycle hook, and MigratorV1V2 does not call setMigrator(0) on completion. So after migration the migrator address retains permanent standing power to drain any user's stake and pending rewards to itself.
impact: Standing centralization / residual-custody hazard. The migrator is a trusted role (Law 3), and the in-scope MigratorV1V2 contract exposes no function that would let an external party trigger such a withdraw/claim (it only ever calls stake), which materially limits exposure. But leaving the role wired after migration is a non-obvious footgun: a competent owner would be surprised that a 'one-shot' migrator keeps god-mode over every position indefinitely. If the migrator is ever an EOA-controlled or upgradeable wrapper, or the key is compromised, all user funds are at risk.
exploitPath: Footgun trigger: migration completes, owner does not call setMigrator(0). Migrator address (M) calls withdraw(user.amount, user) for any user -> user's principal + rewards land in M. Recommendation: call PhlimboV2.setMigrator(address(0)) immediately after migrateDeposits completes (migrateIterator == -1); optionally have MigratorV1V2 expose/automate this.
lawBasis: Law 3 (non-obvious standing-authority footgun) / Law 1 (residual custody over user funds).

title: MigratorV1V2 iterator/accounting/chunking is correct (verification note)
description: VERIFICATION (no defect found in the core iterator/accounting logic). seedObligations is correctly one-shot (require(!seeded) L112, sets seeded=true L139), validates non-empty users (L113) and equal array lengths (L114-119), and precomputes totals consistently with the per-element arrays (L121-138). settleDebt and migrateDeposits use int256 iterators that start at 0, advance by the processed count, and terminate at -1 exactly when i == len (L186-190 / L232-236); the require(iterator >= 0) guards (L157 / L205) correctly block re-entry after completion. Batch bounds are correct: end = min(i + maxIterations, len) (L166-168 / L217-219). Skip-on-zero advances the iterator without paying (L174-183 / L222-229). Across multiple settle batches usdc.balanceOf decrements in lockstep with totalUSDC (L175-176) and phUSD mint does not touch the migrator balance or totalPHUSD_deposited, so the strict-equality invariants are internally self-consistent ABSENT external interference (the external-interference DoS is CODE-012). Across migrate batches, stake pulls dep phUSD from the migrator (V2 L341) while totalPHUSD_deposited decrements by dep (L228), keeping balanceOf == total. forceApprove(max) (L214) is idempotent and safe. No off-by-one, lost-funds, or stuck-state bug was found in this logic itself.
impact: None (positive verification). Recorded so the absence of an accounting bug is auditable. The only correctness/availability issues on this contract are CODE-012 (strict-equality DoS) and CODE-013 (residual custody).
